subsystems.name: Hardware root of trust
subsystems.role: a small tamper-resistant chip that holds keys no software can extract.

subsystems.name: Secure boot chain
subsystems.role: verifies each stage of firmware before it runs, so altered code cannot start.

subsystems.name: Device identity and key management
subsystems.role: gives every device its own certificate so it can prove who it is.

subsystems.name: Secure communications
subsystems.role: encrypts traffic between devices, gateways and cloud services.
parts: MQTT or CoAP brokers with mutual authentication

subsystems.name: Monitoring and anomaly detection
subsystems.role: spots behaviour that departs from a device's normal pattern.
parts: behavioural models running on small microcontrollers

subsystems.name: Update and lifecycle management
subsystems.role: keeps devices patched for a decade or more in the field.

buildSteps.title: Write a threat model
buildSteps.detail: Engineers decide what the device must protect — user data, physical safety, grid or building control — and which attacks are plausible for its 10–20 year life.

buildSteps.title: Choose silicon with a root of trust
buildSteps.detail: The microcontroller or module must include a secure element or TPM plus hardware crypto, because software-only key storage can be read out with physical access.

buildSteps.title: Provision a unique identity
buildSteps.detail: During manufacture, each device generates or receives a private key inside the secure element and is issued its own certificate, so one compromised unit cannot impersonate the fleet.

buildSteps.title: Build the verified boot chain
buildSteps.detail: Firmware images are signed with the vendor's private key; the boot ROM checks each signature before handing control onward.

buildSteps.title: Encrypt the traffic
buildSteps.detail: Sessions use TLS or DTLS with mutual authentication; where bandwidth and RAM are tiny — tens of kilobytes — compact profiles such as OSCORE are used instead.

buildSteps.title: Deploy monitoring
buildSteps.detail: Gateways learn each device's normal message rate, destinations and payload sizes, and raise alerts when a device suddenly talks to new addresses or floods the network.

buildSteps.title: Stand up the update pipeline
buildSteps.detail: Over-the-air updates are signed, versioned, staged to a small group first, and revertible, so a bad release cannot brick a fleet.

buildSteps.title: Operate the security programme
buildSteps.detail: Publish a software bill of materials, track disclosed vulnerabilities, rotate certificates, and wipe keys when devices are retired.

prerequisites.why: battery devices need encryption that costs only a few milliwatts and fits in small memory.
per-device keys are only trustworthy if they live in hardware.
TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.3 and OSCORE let constrained devices speak modern encrypted protocols.
issuing, renewing and revoking millions of certificates is workable but operationally hard and unevenly adopted.
machine-learning models that fit microcontroller budgets exist in research and pilots more than in shipped products.
standards were finalised in 2024, but small, efficient implementations are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: baseline hardening: unique per-device identity, secure boot and encrypted transport
pathway.unlocks: devices that survive casual scanning and botnet recruitment.

pathway.milestone: regulatory labelling and mandatory patching duties in major markets
pathway.unlocks: security as a purchase requirement rather than an afterthought, pushing vendors to ship updates.

pathway.milestone: continuous attestation and network-level zero trust for device fleets
pathway.unlocks: automatic quarantining of a device the moment it misbehaves, without waiting for a human.
infrastructure still trusted long after today's devices are installed.
